title: Oliver's Lincoln Gardens band, Armstrong and sitting in
summary: He heard Oliver's band with the Doddses, Lil Hardin and Armstrong, sat in on Dippermouth Blues, and describes Johnny Dodds.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: Is there anything you can tell us, anything more about Joe Oliver to get back to him? Any other place you heard them? For instance, did you ever hear them at the Royal or Lincoln Gardens? They call them both names.
Yes, yes, I heard them right there. I heard them there, too. Had the band changed?
Do you remember who was in the band in those days?
Well, it was Baby Dots and Johnny Dots and I think so. I think Sincere was in the band. I think a bass player by the name of Johnson.
It was Louie when you heard him down there. Yes, Louie was in that band and Lil Hardin.
Oh, yeah. How did Louie impress you when you first heard him? Wonderful, wonderful. Good the very first time, really?
Oh, yes. He was very good. He played second to Joe. I used to hear Joe play that introduction on West End Blues. I used to hear Joe play that before Louie. Before Louie. Yeah.
He could make all that same stuff that Louie made on the record. Oh, yeah.

Did you ever, did any of you fellow Chicago fellows ever sit in with that band much at the Royal Garden State? Did they ever allow anybody to sit in or did you ever sit in if you remember to play with them?
Well, very few they'd allow sit in to play. And I was one of the privileged few.
Did you play second trumpet to Joe then or how did you work that or what was it? Did you take the lead sometimes?

Yeah, I'd play the Dippermouth Blues and the Riverside Blues and all those tunes. I knew all those tunes. Joe would get a big kick out of it when I'd play the Dippermouth Blues because it's not the Dippermouth Blues unless you play it like Joe.

That's right. Yeah, you still got all that down the same. Oh, yeah. Same words. How did Johnny Dodds impress you? Sometimes he sounds a little rough on records and other times he sounds so great. I just wondered how was he in person in those days? I heard him in late years. Oh, he was a wonderful fellow.

He was a timid soul. He was very nice. I liked his planet playing very much. I believe he used to, you'd think he was afraid of a microphone. And Joe Oliver, he was afraid of a microphone too. He didn't like a microphone. Really? Didn't like? I don't either.

You wouldn't know it because you recorded so much and it sounds great. I remember Rod Kless, your old clarinetist on that Bluebird band that you had, the Ragtime band, told me once he studied a little bit, actually took a couple lessons from Dodds, I think. He used to go down and actually practically study with him, if not actual formal lessons, at least get ideas from him to his home, I think, to study.
